sur0: Always Feeling Cold: Causes, Tests and What You Can Do | İhsan Eren
sur1: Why are you cold when everyone else is comfortable? Possible causes such as thyroid problems, anaemia and Raynaud’s, the tests to ask about, everyday measures and what the evidence says on complementary methods.
sur3: It is natural to feel cold when everyone else does; but if you are always cold while those around you are comfortable, this is called cold intolerance. Most often there is an underlying cause that can be found and corrected, such as an underactive thyroid, anaemia or low body weight, so the first step is a doctor’s examination and a few blood tests. This guide summarises the possible causes, everyday measures and what the evidence says about complementary methods.

sur13: Body temperature is regulated together by thyroid hormones, blood circulation, muscle mass and the layer of fat under the skin. When one of these falls short, you feel colder than other people in the same surroundings. Feeling cold is most often not a disease in itself but a sign of an underlying condition.
sur14: That is why the first thing to do about long-standing or extreme coldness is to see a doctor. If a cause is found, treatment is directed at that cause.
sur16: An underactive thyroid: tiredness, weight gain, constipation and dry skin and hair may accompany feeling cold
sur18: Low body weight and little body fat, especially in thin older women
sur19: Blood vessel problems such as Raynaud’s phenomenon
sur20: Long-term severe illness and poor general health
sur22: Rarely, problems with the part of the brain that sets body temperature (the hypothalamus)
sur23: The first step: examination and tests
sur24: Your doctor takes your history, examines you and usually requests these tests: full blood count, general biochemistry, TSH and thyroid hormones. Other tests may be added depending on your history. Mention the medicines you take as well; some medicines can affect the circulation in the fingers.
sur25: If your fingers clearly change colour, go numb, tingle or hurt in the cold or under stress, this may be Raynaud’s phenomenon. In most people it is harmless; but if the symptoms are severe, affect only one side, started after the age of 30, or come with joint pain, a skin rash and muscle weakness, you should be assessed for an underlying rheumatic condition.
sur26: Normal test results do not mean that your complaint is not real. Some people are constitutionally more sensitive to cold; the measures below can help in that case too. If the complaint changes or new symptoms appear, see your doctor to be reassessed.
sur29: Dress warmly in cold weather, protecting your hands and feet in particular, and keep your home warm.
sur31: Avoid going straight from a warm place into the cold; put your layers on before you go out.
sur33: Regular exercise supports the circulation. In a small study of 16 young women who felt the cold, those who walked and jogged lightly on at least four days a week for two weeks felt less cold in their fingertips and feet; skin temperature did not change.
sur35: Smoking harms the circulation; ask your doctor for support with quitting.
sur37: Cutting down on the caffeine in tea, coffee, cola and chocolate can ease symptoms in some people.
sur39: Stress and anxiety can trigger symptoms; try relaxation methods such as breathing exercises or yoga.
sur41: Eat a balanced diet and eat enough; very low body weight makes you feel colder.
sur42: To relax with your breath, see The 5-minute cyclic sighing breath; to see how much you move in a week, see the weekly activity meter.
sur43: Complementary approaches: what does the evidence say?
sur44: Complementary methods have been studied most in Raynaud’s phenomenon. According to a review of 20 randomised controlled trials:
sur45: Biofeedback: did not work in five trials; the results were no better than sham treatment.
sur46: Heat-retaining (therapeutic) gloves: found helpful in a single trial; how far the result can be generalised is limited.
sur47: Low-level laser: slightly reduced the number of attacks in three trials; the clinical importance of the difference is unclear.
sur48: Acupuncture: there are only two trials; too little data to draw a conclusion.
sur49: Ginkgo biloba, antioxidants and essential fatty acids: no meaningful benefit could be shown, or the data were insufficient.
sur50: The review’s conclusion is clear: well-designed trials are needed, and nothing definite can be said except that biofeedback does not work. Herbal products can interact with medicines; consult your doctor or pharmacist before using them.
sur51: In Turkey, traditional and complementary medicine practices such as acupuncture may be carried out only by doctors who hold a practice certificate in that field, in units authorised by the Ministry of Health. If you would like to try a complementary method, first make sure the underlying cause has been looked into, and think of the method as an addition to medical treatment, not a replacement for it.
sur53: Muscles produce heat as they work. When you feel cold, move for a few minutes instead of staying still; these movements can be done at home or at your desk.
sur54: While sitting, lift your feet slightly off the floor. Pull your toes up towards you, then point them away; keep a lively, rhythmic pace.
sur56: Hold on lightly to the worktop. Lift both heels together, rise onto your toes and lower slowly. This works the calf muscles and gets the circulation in the legs going.
sur59: Hold your hands out in front of you. Make tight fists, then open and stretch your fingers as wide as you can; repeat at a lively pace.
sur61: My tests were normal but I still feel cold. What should I do?
sur62: Normal tests help to rule out the common causes, but they do not make your complaint any less valid. Some people are constitutionally more sensitive to cold. Follow the everyday measures regularly for a few weeks. If the complaint gets worse or new symptoms appear, such as a change in weight, marked tiredness or colour changes in the fingers, see your doctor again.
sur63: My hands and feet are always cold. Is it Raynaud’s?
sur64: Not every cold hand is Raynaud’s. In Raynaud’s, the fingers clearly change colour, go numb, tingle or hurt in the cold or under stress; the symptoms can last from minutes to hours. If there is no colour change, the picture points to cold intolerance rather than Raynaud’s. To be sure, consult your doctor.
sur65: Does acupuncture help with feeling cold?
sur66: There is not enough evidence to say so. In Raynaud’s phenomenon only two small trials have been done, and the review states that no conclusion can be drawn from them. If you would like to try it, first make sure the underlying cause has been looked into. In Turkey, acupuncture may be performed only by doctors certified in this field.
sur68: A small study supports this: among 16 young women who felt the cold, those who walked and jogged lightly on a regular basis for two weeks felt less cold in their fingertips and feet, and their sleep improved too. Because the study was small the result cannot be considered definite; even so, regular activity is a safe step that is worth trying.
sur69: Whiteness or blueness of the fingers that does not go away, a sore or blackening (emergency)
sur70: After being out in the cold: shivering that cannot be stopped, confusion or slowed speech (emergency)
sur71: Feeling cold together with an unexplained change in weight or marked tiredness
sur72: Colour changes in the fingers on one side only, or starting after the age of 30
sur73: Accompanying joint pain, skin rash or muscle weakness
sur74: Pain in the calves when walking, with cold feet or a change in their colour
